note: complete essay, a smaller and more concrete claim

sections.text: The standard advice about comments is that they should say why, not what. It is good advice and it is taught as though the hard part were knowing the rule.
sections.thin: There is a common piece of advice about writing comments.

sections.text: The comments worth writing are the ones recording a decision you argued about, and almost nothing else survives contact with a codebase.

A comment explaining what the code does has a half-life of about one refactor. A comment saying we tried the obvious thing and it deadlocked under load is still true in five years, because it is about the world rather than about the code.
sections.thin: There are several considerations that can be put forward in support of this idea, and taken together they paint a reasonably coherent picture of the situation as it can be observed in most software development contexts.

sections.text: It also explains why comment rot feels worse than missing comments: a stale what-comment actively lies, whereas a stale why-comment at worst describes a road not taken.
A reasonable objection is that newcomers need the what-comments most, and writing for the reader who already knows the system is how codebases become unapproachable.

That need is real but it is a documentation need, not a comment need. A newcomer reads a file top to bottom once; a maintainer reads a hunk in a diff a hundred times, and the comment is in the second person's field of view, not the first's.
sections.thin: I think there is an answer to that.
